description: Sky cues (A-07, B-06, ADR-0018): qualitative colors of skies and twilight that the stylized style draws, each with the sentence of its source that states it. A cue names a hue from a fixed vocabulary; the colors that draw the hues are display choices (docs/ART_DIRECTION.md section 5). Whether a body has an atmosphere at all comes from the pack's surface conditions through the core, not from this file. Written by `usim-pipeline sky-cues` to UniverseSim/Assets/UniverseSim/Data/SkyCues.json.

cues.reference: Pieters et al. (1986), Science 234, abstract (NASA Technical Reports Server record 19870039592)
cues.quote: Multispectral images of the basaltic surface of Venus obtained by Venera 13 were processed to remove the effects of orange-colored incident radiation resulting from interactions with the thick Venusian atmosphere.
cues.note: The light reaching the surface is orange; the cue's meaning includes daylight at the surface (ADR-0018).

cues.reference: NASA Space Place, 'Why Is the Sky Blue?'
cues.quote: This is why we see a blue sky most of the time.
cues.note: Tier 2, labeled: no Tier 1 statement of the daytime sky's color was found in an accessible form.

cues.reference: NASA Earth Observatory, 'Sundown and Lights Up Over the U.S. Northeast', astronaut photograph ISS070-E-76065
cues.quote: The troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere, appears red and yellow.
cues.note: The caption describes the limb as the Sun dips below the curvature of the Earth: 'As the Sun dips below the curvature of Earth, the varying layers of the atmosphere appear as different hues in this oblique photograph of Earth’s limb.'

cues.reference: NASA/JPL, PIA01547, 'True Color of Mars - Pathfinder Sol 24 at 4 PM'
cues.quote: The brownish gray sky as it would be seen by an observer on Mars in this four-frame, true color mosaic taken on sol 24 (at approximately 1610 LST).
cues.note: The same caption: 'The sky near the sun is a pale blue color.' PIA00917 adds that the dust 'absorbs blue light, giving the sky its red color'.

cues.reference: NASA/JPL, PIA00917, 'Color Variations in the Sky at Sunset'
cues.quote: The blue color only becomes apparent near sunrise and sunset, when the light has to pass through the largest amount of dust.
cues.note: The same caption: 'The blue color near the Sun is not caused by clouds of water ice, but by the martian dust itself.' Curiosity saw the same (NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/Texas A&M Univ., PIA19400).
